FOR NUISANCE WILDLIFE CONTROL OPERATORS

The ad prices one visit. You are making eight.

The “$395 raccoon removal” your customer is holding pays for one trip. The job you actually sold is an inspection, an install, a trap check every day the traps are out, a trip back to pull the one-way door, sixty feet of seal at a two-story eave, an attic to clean, and three years of warranty you have not reserved a dollar against. Price the visits, not the animal.

What should I charge for a wildlife exclusion job? — the worked example in full

Compare: this calculator vs. PestPac, or this calculator vs. a flat $395 removal fee.

The job

Species sets the starting footage and decides whether this job has trapping in it at all — bats and birds are excluded through one-way devices, never trapped. The month is used only to flag a maternity-season schedule.

Crew and the drive

Drive time is paid time, and it is charged on every visit — both legs. The trap-check crew is separate because the tech who checks a trap is usually not the two-person crew that did the seal.

Trapping

Checks per day is your figure, not a rule this tool asserts — most states require every 24 hours. Set trap days to 0 for a pure exclusion job.

The seal

This is the part the warranty covers, and the only part the height tier multiplies.

    A bid link carries this whole job — species, height, trap and exclusion figures, your rates — so it reopens exactly as you left it. The numbers ride after the #, which is never sent to a server, so copying a link uploads nothing.

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      Why does this ask how many days the traps are out?

      Because every one of those days is a return trip. Traps that are set have to be checked, and most states require it every 24 hours. A five-day raccoon removal is five more round trips with a technician in the truck, on top of the install visit and the trip back to pull the one-way door. That recurring visit is the single largest cost a flat removal fee omits, and it is why matching a competitor’s headline number loses money by day three.

      Why is height a multiplier instead of a line item?

      Because it changes how long the same footage takes, not what it costs in material. Sixty feet of soffit-to-roof line reachable from a step ladder is a different job from the same sixty feet at a two-story eave on a steep pitch in a harness, and different again where nothing but a lift will reach it. Per-foot pricing that ignores the tier is wrong by a factor, in the same direction, every time. The multiplier applies only to the exclusion and one-way-door work — it does not touch trap checks in the yard or decontamination in the attic, which take the same time however high the roof is.

      Why does the warranty reserve only cover part of the job?

      Because a callback is somebody returning to a hole that reopened, not to an attic that was already cleaned. The reserve here is taken against the work the warranty actually covers — the exclusion labor, the exclusion material and the devices — rather than against the whole invoice. Reserving against decontamination and trapping would inflate the price for exposure you do not carry; reserving against nothing at all means the first callback comes out of the profit on the next job.

      Does this tell me when I am allowed to exclude bats?

      No, and it must not be read that way. It flags that a job is scheduled in a month when the species you picked commonly has flightless or immobile young, because sealing the entry then can trap them inside — which is both an animal-welfare problem and, in many states, prohibited. The actual window is set by your state wildlife agency, varies by latitude and species, and changes. Treat the flag as a prompt to go and check with your agency before you schedule, never as a determination that any date is or is not permitted.

      Why does a bat job show no traps?

      Because bats are not trapped. They are excluded live through one-way devices that let them leave and not return, and the job is the seal plus the device removal trip, not a trapping cycle. The calculator flags a bat or bird job that has been given traps, because that is a trapping rate sheet applied to an animal nobody traps — and it usually means the visit count, which is the number that decides whether the bid is sound, was built for the wrong job.

      Is any of this uploaded?

      No. There is no account and the page makes no network requests — it runs entirely in your browser. The address, the species, your labor rate, your footage and the price worked out from them are never sent anywhere and never appear in a usage count. The optional counter records only which features were used and the day, stored on your own device, and it switches itself off for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

      Is this legal, wildlife-regulation, or insurance advice?

      No. It is arithmetic on the figures you type. It makes no determination about what your state’s wildlife code requires, how often traps must be checked, whether a species may be excluded on a given date, what licence or permit a job needs, or what to charge. Verify every figure and every requirement against your own costs, your state wildlife agency, and a qualified professional before sending a bid.

      No warranty. This free tool is not legal, wildlife-regulation, veterinary, tax, financial, or insurance advice, and it does not tell you what to charge, how often traps must be checked, whether a species may lawfully be excluded on a given date, or what licence, permit or coverage a job needs. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type, and the numbers it starts with are an illustrative example rather than market data. Verify every figure against your own costs, your state wildlife agency, and a qualified professional before sending a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

      Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. The address, species, rates, footage and the price worked out here are never uploaded and never appear in a usage count — those are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally, and switched off automatically for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control. The six events counted are bid_calculated, flat_fee_compared, proposed_price_compared, proposal_printed, company_forgotten and link_copied — names and a date, never a figure.

      What the proposal saves, and what it never does. Your own business block — company name, phone, email, licence, address — is kept in this browser so you type it once. The customer’s name and address are not saved: that is someone else’s personal data, and it is re-typed per job on purpose. “Forget my business details” deletes the stored block. The proposal prints only your own words and numbers; it drafts no legal terms, warranty language or cancellation rights, and it is not a contract.

      Pricing a different kind of route or project? The pest control bid calculator prices a recurring account per stop rather than a one-off project, and the attic insulation bid calculator prices the R-value side of the same attic.

vs-a-flat-395-removal-fee.html.text:
← Wildlife Exclusion Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $395 removal fee

"$395 removal fee" is not a price for a wildlife exclusion job — it is a price for one visit and one trap, quietly reused for every attic the truck rolls out to, whatever it actually holds.

What a flat $395 removal fee is

A flat removal fee is the fastest way to advertise: one number, easy to post online and easy for a homeowner to compare between companies. It is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's ad will call and ask a shop to match, whatever the attic actually needs.

The number behind it was set for one job — a single visit, a single trap or a ladder, and nothing to clean up afterward — and then reused for every job afterward, whether or not the next attic looks anything like the one it was priced on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the species, the height tier the exclusion work is reached at — ground level up through a lift — how many days traps stay out and how many checks a day, linear feet of exclusion and one-way devices and the trip back to pull them, attic decontamination and insulation by the square foot, disposal, repairs, and a reserve sized against a multi-year warranty. It prices the visits, the height, and every extra separately, and returns a walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this job, not a generic one.

What a flat $395 removal fee doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same fee whether the job is one visit for a ground-level groundhog with a single trap, or a raccoon job with five days of daily trap checks and a two-story seal. Prices the trap days, checks per day, and height tier from what was entered, so the two jobs above come out at different numbers instead of one.
Has no line for a return trip, so a job needing daily trap checks for five days gets quoted the same as a job needing one visit and done. Counts every trap-check visit and prices its own drive time and labor, so five days of checks cost more than none.
Assumes ground level, so a two-story eave in a harness or a job that needs a lift gets quoted the same as work reachable from the ground. Applies a height-tier multiplier to exclusion and one-way-device labor, so a lift job costs more than a ground-level one.
Has no line for a one-way device's removal trip, attic decontamination, insulation replacement, or a warranty reserve, regardless of how much the job needs. Prices each of those separately from its own inputs, so a fully loaded job costs more than a bare removal.
Gives the shop an ad price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when a homeowner asks to match a cheaper one-visit special on a multi-day job. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against the flat fee, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

Three jobs, the same removal fee

At this calculator's own shop-rate defaults ($25/hr crew wage, 52% payroll burden, 14% overhead on direct cost, a 22% target margin, $0.85/mile and 22 drive minutes each way, a 3-year warranty reserved at 8%):

JobThis calculator's break-even costThe flat $395 feeGap
Groundhog, ground level, one trap, one check, no decontamination$645.18$395.00The fee prices $250.18 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit.
Raccoon, two-story seal, five days of daily trap checks, one one-way door, 250 sq ft of attic decontamination — this calculator's own default job$2,740.42$395.00The fee prices $2,345.42 below break-even.
Bat, lift required, three one-way devices, 400 sq ft of decontamination and insulation replacement$4,866.77$395.00The fee prices $4,471.77 below break-even.

The flat fee is a fixed $395.00, not derived from any of the three jobs. It does not clear even the cheapest one: a single-visit, ground-level groundhog job with one trap and no decontamination — the kind of job a $395 ad is set on — still prices above the fee at these shop rates. Run your own job's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat fee is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied without checking it against a real cost base, and nothing about an ad price tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat fee skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $395 removal fee get a bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is visits, height, and decontamination, not "an animal removal" alone. A one-visit, ground-level groundhog job is a different job from a raccoon job with five days of daily trap checks, a two-story seal reached with an extension ladder, a one-way door and the trip back to pull it, and an attic to decontaminate -- and a flat removal number cannot see which one it is looking at.

What does a flat removal fee usually leave out entirely?

The trap-check visits, the height-tier labor, the one-way device and its removal trip, the decontamination and insulation, and the warranty reserve. A published removal fee is priced on one visit and one trap or one ladder -- it has nowhere to put the hours for four more days of checks, a harness at a steep pitch, a lift, or an attic full of contaminated insulation.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shop-rate defaults ($25/hr crew wage, 52% burden, 14% overhead, a 22% target margin, $0.85/mile and 22 drive minutes each way): a one-visit, ground-level groundhog job with a single trap and no decontamination has a $645.18 break-even cost, already $250.18 above the flat $395 before a dollar of profit. This calculator's own default raccoon job -- a two-story seal, five days of daily trap checks, one one-way door, and 250 square feet of attic decontamination -- breaks even at $2,740.42. A bat job needing a lift, three one-way devices, and 400 square feet of decontamination breaks even at $4,866.77.

Is a flat removal fee ever the right way to quote a wildlife exclusion job?

Not on this calculator's own numbers, even for the cheapest job in the comparison: a single one-visit, ground-level groundhog job with one trap and no decontamination already breaks even above the flat $395, before a single day of trap checks, a ladder, or an attic full of insulation enters the bid. The fee is not close on the hard case -- it is already short on the easy one.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local labor rates, wildlife-control pricing, or what any state permits. It takes the species, the height tier the work is reached at, trap days and checks per day, one-way devices, decontamination and insulation by the square foot, disposal, repairs, and your loaded labor and warranty reserve, and turns them into a walk-away price for the job you describe -- the arithmetic a flat fee skips, not a market survey.

Open the Wildlife Exclusion Bid Calculator to price your own job, or read what should I charge for a wildlife exclusion job.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, wildlife-regulation, veterinary, tax, financial, or insurance advice, and it does not tell you what to charge, how often traps must be checked, whether a species may lawfully be excluded on a given date, or what licence, permit or coverage a job needs. Verify every figure against your own costs, your state wildlife agency, and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number on this page and in the calculator stays on this device; this page names no company, product, or service, so it makes no claim about how anyone else prices a job.

Free and open source. If it wins you a job, the code is under an MIT licence — support via GitHub Sponsors is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

This calculator vs. PestPac

Two different shapes: PestPac is an account-based platform for running a wildlife or pest control company's whole operation, including scheduling and billing an exclusion job once it is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this exclusion job cost, given its trap days, height, devices and warranty, before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

PestPac, sold by WorkWave, is a field service management platform used by pest and nuisance wildlife control businesses, from single-truck operators to national multi-branch companies, to run CRM and customer records, scheduling and routing, billing and payments, marketing, reporting, and a technician mobile app, tied to one account used on an ongoing paid basis across every job the company runs. PestPac's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that scheduling and billing software describe routing, dispatching and invoicing a job once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a wildlife exclusion job should cost from trap-check visits, height tier, one-way devices, decontamination and warranty reserve before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what PestPac does. It does not store a customer record, build a route across a season, or invoice anyone. what-to-charge-for-wildlife-exclusion.ht.text:
NUISANCE WILDLIFE CONTROL PRICING

What should I charge for a wildlife exclusion job?

The homeowner who called you has a browser tab open on a “$395 raccoon removal” ad, and they are going to ask why you are not that. The honest answer is that the ad prices catching an animal and you are quoting ending the problem — but “it’s more work” is not an answer anybody buys. A visit count is.

This page works one job all the way through. The wildlife exclusion bid calculator does the same arithmetic on your own numbers, in your browser, with nothing uploaded.

Open the calculator

The job

A raccoon in the attic of a two-story house. A separate inspection trip, then three traps set for five days with a check on each day, 45 linear feet of soffit and roof line sealed at the two-story eave, one one-way door with a trip back to pull it, 250 square feet of attic decontaminated, insulation removed and replaced over the same area, a disposal ticket, some chewed soffit repaired, and three years of warranty on the seal.

The crew is two people on a $25 wage carrying a 52% payroll burden — $38 an hour each once workers’ comp for at-height work is in it; one of them goes alone on the trap checks. The shop is 14 miles out, 22 minutes each way, and the truck costs $0.85 a mile.

Start with the visits, because that is the argument

VisitHow manyWho goes
Inspection12
Install: set traps, seal, hang the one-way door12
Trap check, one per day the traps are out51
Pull the device, close the last hole12
Total round trips8—

Eight round trips at 14 miles each way is 224 miles, and 22 minutes each way is $306.53 of paid drive time — more than the entire on-site trapping labor. The flat removal fee prices one of those eight trips. That is the whole gap, and it is visible before anyone argues about rates.

It is also why the calculator asks how many days the traps stay out rather than asking for a trapping price. Most states require a set trap to be checked every 24 hours; each of those checks is a truck leaving the shop.

Every line

LineAmount
Driving, all eight visits$306.53
Inspection on site (45 min, 2 people)$57.00
Seal and device labor (45 ft × 1.4 min × 1.7 for two-story, plus the door)$264.86
Trapping and checks on site$124.77
Attic decontamination labor (250 sq ft)$142.50
Labor subtotal$895.66
Vehicle, 224 miles at $0.85$190.40
Seal material (45 ft × $3.20), device, bait$210.00
Decontamination material (PPE, disinfectant, bags)$137.50
Insulation: 250 sq ft out at $1.40, back in at $1.90$825.00
Disposal and soffit repair$250.00
Direct cost$2,508.56
Warranty reserve, 8% of the $453.86 of warranted work$36.31
Overhead at 14% of direct cost$351.20
Walk-away price$2,896.07
Bid at a 22% net margin$3,712.91

23.6 crew hours, so the bid is $157.53 per crew hour. That is the number to sanity-check against your own shop, because it is the one figure here that does not move when you change how the job is described.

Three things this ordering should change

The attic is the biggest line, and it is the one that gets dropped

Insulation is $825 — the largest single line on the job, larger than any labor line. It is also the line a nervous operator offers to remove when the customer flinches at the total, because it feels like an upsell. Removing it does not make the bid competitive with a $395 ad; it makes a $3,712.91 bid into a $2,700 bid that leaves contaminated insulation in an attic somebody's children sleep under.

Height is a multiplier, not a surcharge

The same 45 feet of seal is $155.80 of labor at ground level and $264.86 at a two-story eave. If you price exclusion per linear foot from a single rate, every two-story house you bid is wrong by that factor, in the same direction. A per-foot rate sheet is fine as long as it has tiers in it.

The reserve is small, and zero is not

Eight percent of the warranted work is $36.31 on this job — less than the disposal ticket. Almost nobody carries it, so the first callback in year two comes out of the profit on whatever job is running that week. Sizing it against the seal and the device rather than against the whole invoice is what keeps it small enough to actually charge.

What this does not tell you

It does not tell you when you may exclude. The calculator flags a job scheduled in a month when the species you picked commonly has young that cannot leave on their own, because sealing then traps them inside — but the actual window is set by your state wildlife agency, varies by latitude and species, and changes. The flag is a prompt to go and check before you put a date on the calendar. It is not a determination that any date is or is not permitted, and this page is not a substitute for your agency or your licence conditions.

Price your own job

Common questions

What should I charge for a wildlife exclusion job?

Far more than the flat removal fee homeowners shop against. On the worked example on this page — a raccoon in a two-story attic, three traps out for five days, 45 feet of seal, 250 square feet of decontamination and insulation replacement, and a three-year warranty — the walk-away price is $2,896.07 and the bid at a 22% net margin is $3,712.91. The $395 removal ad the customer is holding is $2,501.07 short of what the job costs to do, because it prices one visit and the job is eight.

Why is the flat removal fee so far off?

Because it prices catching an animal, and the job is ending the problem. The removal fee covers one trip. This job carries an inspection trip, an install trip, a trap check on each of five days, and a trip back to pull the one-way door — eight round trips, 224 miles and $306.53 of paid drive time before anyone has touched the roof. Add the seal, the attic and the warranty reserve and the arithmetic is not close.

Which single line costs the most?

Insulation, at $825 — 250 square feet removed at $1.40 and replaced at $1.90. Labor as a whole is larger at $895.66, but no single labor line beats it; the closest is driving, at $306.53. That ordering is worth knowing because it is the opposite of how these jobs get quoted: operators negotiate hardest over the trapping, which is $124.77 of on-site labor here, and treat the attic restoration as an add-on the customer can decline.

Why does the height of the work change the labor by that much?

Because reaching the work is most of the work. The same 45 feet of seal costs $155.80 of labor at ground level and $264.86 at a two-story eave on an extension ladder — a 1.7x multiplier applied to the exclusion and device time only, not to trap checks in the yard or decontamination in the attic. An operator pricing per linear foot from a single rate is wrong by that factor, in the same direction, on every two-story house they bid.

What is the warranty reserve for?

A callback. This job was sold with three years on the exclusion, and a callback is a truck, a technician and a ladder returning to a hole that reopened. The reserve here is 8% of the warranted work only — the exclusion labor, the exclusion material and the device, $453.86 between them — which comes to $36.31. That figure is small enough to be painless and specific enough to be honest, which is more than can be said for the usual reserve of zero.

Is any of this legal or wildlife-regulation advice?

No. It is arithmetic on the figures entered. It makes no determination about what your state’s wildlife code requires, how often traps must be checked, whether a species may lawfully be excluded on a given date, or what licence or permit a job needs. Verify every figure and every requirement against your own costs, your state wildlife agency, and a qualified professional before sending a bid.
